facts.text: I discussed “The Depreciated Legacy of Cervantes,” Part 5.
I compared war in Homer and Tolstoy to war in Schweik and his companions.
I argued that Schweik and his companions go to the front without knowing why.
I argued that Schweik and his companions go to the front without caring to know.
I questioned what the motor of war is if not Helen or country.
I suggested that war could be driven by sheer force that wills to assert itself as force.
I referenced Heidegger’s idea of the “will to will.”
I claimed that in Hasek, force is stripped of any rational argument.
I stated that no one believes the propaganda in Hasek, not even those who manufacture it.
I stated that force is naked in Hasek, like force in Kafka’s novels.
I asked why Germany and Russia want to dominate the world.
I stated that the aggressivity of force is disinterested, unmotivated, and wills only its own will.
I said Kafka and Hasek present a paradox about the Modern Era: Cartesian rationality corroding inherited Middle Ages values.
I stated that pure irrationality seizes the world stage when there is no longer any generally accepted value system to block it.
I said this paradox is illuminated in Hermann Broch’s The Sleepwalkers.
I said I like to call the paradox “terminal.”
I stated that the Modern Era nurtured a dream of mankind uniting in unity and everlasting peace.
I stated that today the history of the planet has become one indivisible whole, but war embodies and guarantees unity of mankind.
I stated that unity of mankind means no escape for anyone anywhere.
I referenced Husserl’s lectures on the European crisis and on the possible disappearance of European mankind.
I stated that Husserl gave those lectures in two capitals of Central Europe.
I stated that in Central Europe the West could see the death of the West, or the amputation of a part of itself.
I stated that Warsaw, Budapest, and Prague were swallowed up by the Russian empire.
I stated that this calamity was engendered by the First World War.
I stated that the First World War was unleashed by the Hapsburg empire.
I stated that the First World War led to the end of the Hapsburg empire.
I stated that the First World War unbalanced forever an enfeebled Europe.
I stated that the peaceful time of Joyce and Proust involved man grappling only with the monster of his own soul.
I stated that in the novels of Kafka, Hasek, Musil, and Broch, the monster comes from outside and is called History.
I stated that History in those novels is impersonal, uncontrollable, incalculable, incomprehensible, and inescapable.
I stated that just after the First World War, a group of great Central European novelists saw, felt, and grasped the terminal paradoxes of the Modern Era.
I discussed “The Depreciated Legacy of Cervantes,” Part 6.
I stated that Central Europe was where the West could see the death of the West or the amputation of part of itself when Warsaw, Budapest, and Prague were swallowed up by the Russian empire.
I stated that the calamity was engendered by the First World War unleashed by the Hapsburg empire.
I stated that the First World War led to the end of the Hapsburg empire and unbalanced an enfeebled Europe forever.
I stated that in the novels of Kafka, Hasek, Musil, and Broch, the monster comes from outside and is called History.
I stated that History is impersonal, uncontrollable, incalculable, incomprehensible, and inescapable in those novels.
I stated that just after the First World War, the pleiad of great Central European novelists grasped the terminal paradoxes of the Modern Era.
I argued it would be wrong to read these novels as social and political prophecies like Orwell.
I stated that Orwell’s message could have been said in an essay or pamphlet.
I stated that these novelists discover “what only the novel can discover.”
I stated that under the conditions of the terminal paradoxes, existential categories suddenly change their meaning.
I asked what adventure is if K.’s freedom of action is completely illusory.
I asked what future is if the intellectuals of The Man Without Qualities have no inkling of the war that will sweep their lives away the next day.
I asked what crime is if Broch’s Huguenau does not regret but actually forgets the murder he has committed.
I stated that Hasek’s Schweik uses war as its setting and asked where the difference between public and private is if K. is never without the two emissaries of the Castle even in bed with a woman.
I asked what solitude is if K. is never without the two emissaries of the Castle even in bed with a woman.
I stated that solitude can be seen as a burden, misery, or curse, or as a supremely precious value in the process of being crushed by ubiquitous collectivity.
I stated that the periods of the novel’s history are very long and characterized by the particular aspect on which the novel concentrates.
I stated that Flaubert’s discovery of the quotidian was only fully developed seventy years later in James Joyce’s work.
I stated that the period inaugurated seventy years ago by the pleiad of Central European novelists (the period of terminal paradoxes) seems far from finished.
